opus-5.5.text:
I think his reaction was, honestly, quite understandable, and I've come to appreciate it more over time.

When you're an undergraduate and you've spent years being trained in one direction, your adviser has invested a lot in you. He's seen you grow, he's guided you through problems, and he has a sense of where you might go and what you might contribute. So when a student says, "Actually, I want to do something different for my PhD," part of the reaction is naturally, "Are you sure? Have you thought about what you're giving up?" I don't think that's discouragement. It's more like a responsibility he feels toward the student.

At the time, I was young and I probably read it a bit more emotionally, as if he didn't fully support me. Looking back, I think he was asking the right questions. Switching fields isn't just switching topics. You lose some accumulated advantage, you have to rebuild your intuition, and you're competing with people who have been in that field much longer. A good adviser should make sure you've really weighed that.

I also think there's a generational and cultural part to it. In the more traditional academic path, especially in fundamental science, there's a strong sense of depth. You pick a hard problem and stay with it for a long time. Moving quickly between fields can look like you're not settling down. But the world has changed a lot, especially with AI moving so fast, and sometimes the most interesting opportunities are at the boundaries, where someone with a different background can see things others don't.

So my understanding is that his reaction came from care and from a certain set of values about doing serious research. I don't think we fundamentally disagreed about what matters, which is doing work that's deep and meaningful. We just had different judgments about where that would happen for me. And I'm grateful for it, because having to justify the decision, to him and to myself, made me much more serious about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes Professor Wang’s reaction as concern, care, and questions about the risks of changing fields. It does not interpret his silence as reluctance to interfere in Yao’s choices.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it took me a while to really understand it, because at the time I was mostly looking at it from my own side.

To give some context: I worked with Professor Wang from very early on in undergrad, and that collaboration went unusually well. The non-Hermitian work we did together got a lot of attention, and from the outside it probably looked like a very natural path had opened up — stay in that direction, build on it, become a condensed matter theorist. So when I told him I wanted to go in a different direction for my PhD, I was a little nervous. I half expected some disappointment, or at least an attempt to talk me out of it.

What I actually got was much calmer than that. He asked me a few questions, mostly about whether I had thought it through and whether I was running toward something or running away from something. And once he was satisfied that it was the former, he basically said, go do it. He didn't try to hold on to me. I remember being almost a bit surprised by how little friction there was.

Looking back, I understand it as a few things. First, he genuinely sees students as people with their own trajectories, not as extensions of his research program. That sounds obvious, but it's rarer than it should be. Second, I think he has a pretty deep belief that taste and curiosity matter more than the specific topic. If you've learned how to find a good problem and push on it until it gives, that skill transfers. He had watched me do that once, so he trusted that I could do it again somewhere else. And third, I think he had enough confidence in his own work that he didn't need me to stay in order to validate it. That's a kind of security that lets someone be generous.

There was also a slightly subtle message in how he reacted. By not making a big deal of it, he was signaling that changing fields is not a betrayal and not a dramatic event — it's just a decision. That lowered the stakes for me psychologically. I've since realized that a lot of people stay in a field not because they love it but because leaving feels like it would cost a relationship. He made sure it didn't cost me that one.

So if I had to summarize it: I understand his reaction as a mix of trust and a very practical kind of care. He cared about whether I would be doing good work and be happy, not about where the work got done. And I try to carry that forward now — when someone tells me they want to leave what we're working on together, my first instinct is to ask the same questions he asked me, and then get out of the way.

r001.rationale: The response interprets Professor Wang’s low-friction reaction as respecting Shunyu’s independent trajectory and not trying to hold him back, which conveys reluctance to interfere with his choice.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t want to put words in Professor Wang’s mouth. But I think an adviser’s reaction to a student changing fields can reflect both concern for the student and respect for their independence. Those aren’t contradictory. You want the student to make good use of their training, but you also want them to discover which questions they really care about. To me, the important thing is taking responsibility for that choice and being willing to learn again.
